transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: Hello, Wayside Camera Club, Breda speaking.

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: Oh, hello, um, my name's Dan and I'd like to join your club.

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: That's great, Dan. We have an application form – would you like to complete it over the phone, then you can ask any questions you might have?

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: Oh, yes, thanks.

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: OK, so what's your family name?

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: It's Green – Dan Green.

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: So – can I take your email address?

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: Yes, it's dan1068@market.com.

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: Thanks. And what about your home address?

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: Well, I'm about ten miles away from your club in Peacetown. I live in a house there.

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: OK, so what's the house number and street?

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: It's 52 <q id="1">Marrowfield Street.</q>

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: Is that M-A double R-O-W-F-I-E-L-D?

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: That's right.

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: … and that's Peacetown, you said?

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: Uhuh.

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: So how did you hear about our club? Did you look on the internet?

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: I usually do that, but this time, well, <q id="2">I was talking to a relative</q> the other day and he suggested it.

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: Oh, is he a member too?

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: He belongs to another club – but he'd heard good things about yours.

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: OK. So what do you hope to get from joining?

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: Well, one thing that really interests me is the competitions that you have. I enjoy entering those.

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: Right. Anything else?

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: Well, <q id="3">I also like to socialise</q> with other photographers.

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: That's great. So what type of membership would you like?

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: What are the options?

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: It's <q id="4">£30 a year for full membership</q> or £20 a year if you're an associate.

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: I think I'll go for the full membership, then.

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: That's a good idea because you can't vote in meetings with an associate membership.

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: If I could just find out a bit more about you …

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: So you said you wanted to compete – have you ever won any photography competitions?

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: Not yet, but I have entered three in the past.

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: Oh, that's interesting. So why don't you tell me something about those? Let's start with the first one.

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: Well, <q id="5">the theme was entitled 'Domestic Life'.</q>

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: I see – so it had to be something related to the home?

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: Yeah. I chose to take a photo of a family sitting round the dinner table having a meal, and, um, I didn't win, but I did get some feedback.

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: Oh, what did the judges say?

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: That it was too 'busy' as a picture.

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: Aha – so it was the composition of the picture that they criticised?

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: That's right – and once they'd told me that, I could see my mistake.

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: So what was the theme of the second competition?

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: Well, my university was on the coast and that area gets a lot of beautiful sunsets, so that was the theme.

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: Oh, sunsets, that's a great theme.

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: Yes. <q id="6">The instructions were to capture the clouds as well</q> – it couldn't just be blue sky and a setting sun.

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: Sure, cause they give you all those amazing pinks and purples.

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: Yeah – and I thought I'd done that well, but the feedback was that I should have waited a bit longer to get the shot.

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: I see. So <q id="7">the timing wasn't right.</q>

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: Yes – I took it too soon, basically. And then <q id="8">the third competition I entered was called 'Animal Magic'.</q>

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: Well, that's a difficult subject!

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: I know! I had to take hundreds of shots.

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: I'm sure – because animals move all the time.

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: That's what we had to show – <q id="9">there had to be some movement in the scene.</q> I got a great shot of a fox in the end, but I took it at night and, well, <q id="10">I suspected that it was a bit dark, which is what I was told.</q>

transcript.speaker: BREDA
transcript.text: Well Dan – you seem to be really keen and we'd be delighted to have you in our club. I'm sure we can help with all those areas that you've outlined.

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: Thanks, that's great.

transcript.speaker: PRESENTER
transcript.text: This evening we're delighted to welcome Dan Beagle, who's just written a book on looking for and finding food in the wild. He's going to tell us everything we need to know about picking wild mushrooms.

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: Thank you very much. Well, I need to start by talking about safety. You really need to know what you're doing because some mushrooms are extremely poisonous. Having said that, once you know what to look for, it's really worth doing for the amazing variety of mushrooms available – which you can't get in the shops. But of course, you have to be very careful and that's why I always say <q id="11">you should never consume mushrooms picked by friends or neighbours</q> – always remember that some poisonous mushrooms look very similar to edible ones and it's easy for people to get confused. The other thing to <q id="12">avoid is mushrooms growing beside busy</q> roads for obvious reasons. But nothing beats the taste of freshly picked mushrooms – don't forget that the ones in the shops are often several days old and past their best.

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: There are certain ideas about wild mushrooms that it's important to be aware of. Don't listen to people who tell you that <q id="13">it's only OK to eat mushrooms that are pale or dull – this is completely untrue. Some edible mushrooms are bright red,</q> for example. Personally, I prefer mushrooms cooked but it won't do you any harm to eat them uncooked in salads – it's not necessary to peel them. Another thing you should remember is that you can't tell if a mushroom is safe to eat by its smell – some of the most deadly mushrooms have no smell and taste quite nice, apparently. Finally, <q id="14">just because deer or squirrels eat a particular mushroom doesn't mean that you can.</q>

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: Of course, mushroom picking is associated with the countryside but if you haven't got a car, your local park can be a great place to start. There are usually a range of habitats where mushrooms grow, such as playing fields and wooded areas. But <q id="15">you need to be there first thing in the morning,</q> as there's likely be a lot of competition – not just from people but wildlife too. The deer often get the best mushrooms in my local park.

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: If you're a complete beginner, I wouldn't recommend going alone or relying on photos in a book, even the one I've written! There are some really good phone apps for identifying mushrooms, but you can't always rely on getting a good signal in the middle of a wood. <q id="16">If possible, you should go with a group led by an expert</q> – you'll stay safe and learn a lot that way.

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: Conservation is a really important consideration and you must follow a few basic rules. <q id="17">You should never pick all the mushrooms in one area – collect only enough for your own needs.</q> Be very careful that you don't trample on young mushrooms or other plants. And make sure you don't pick any mushrooms that are endangered and protected by law.

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: There's been a decline in some varieties of wild mushrooms in this part of the country. Restaurants are becoming more interested in locally sourced food like wild mushrooms, but <q id="18">the biggest problem is that so many new houses have been built in this area in the last ten years.</q> And more water is being taken from rivers and reservoirs because of this, and mushroom habitats have been destroyed.

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: Anyway, a word of advice on storing mushrooms. Collect them in a brown paper bag and as soon as you get home, put them in the fridge. <q id="19">They'll be fine for a couple of days, but it's best to cook them as soon as possible</q> – after washing them really carefully first, of course.

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: So everybody knows what a mushroom tastes like, right? Well, you'll be surprised by the huge variety of wild mushrooms there are. Be adventurous! <q id="20">They're great in so many dishes – stir fries, risottos, pasta.</q> But just be aware that some people can react badly to certain varieties so it's a good idea not to eat huge quantities to begin with.

transcript.speaker: DAN
transcript.text: OK, so now I'm going to show you …

transcript.speaker: YOUNG MAN
transcript.text: That seminar yesterday on automation and the future of work was really good, wasn't it? Looking at the first industrial revolution in Britain in the 19th century and seeing how people reacted to massive change was a real eye-opener.

transcript.speaker: YOUNG WOMAN
transcript.text: Yes. It was interesting to hear how people felt about automation then and what challenges they faced. I didn't know that first started with workers in the textile industry.

transcript.speaker: YOUNG MAN
transcript.text: With those protesting workers called the Luddites destroying their knitting machines because they were so worried about losing their jobs.

transcript.speaker: YOUNG WOMAN
transcript.text: Yes, and <q id="21">ultimately, they didn't achieve anything.</q> And anyway, industrialisation created more jobs than it destroyed.

transcript.speaker: YOUNG MAN
transcript.text: Yes, that's true – but <q id="22">it probably didn't seem a positive thing at the time. I can see why the Luddites felt so threatened.</q>

transcript.speaker: YOUNG WOMAN
transcript.text: I know. I'm sure I would have felt the same. The discussion about the future of work was really optimistic for a change. I like the idea that work won't involve doing boring, repetitive tasks, as robots will do all that. Normally, you only hear negative stuff about the future.

transcript.speaker: YOUNG MAN
transcript.text: Bit too optimistic, don't you think? For example, I can't see how people are about to have more leisure time, when <q id="23">all the evidence shows people are spending longer than ever at work.</q>

transcript.speaker: YOUNG WOMAN
transcript.text: No – that's true. And what about <q id="24">lower unemployment? I'm not so sure about that.</q>

transcript.speaker: YOUNG MAN
transcript.text: Perhaps in the long term – but not in the foreseeable future.

transcript.speaker: YOUNG WOMAN
transcript.text: Mmm. And I expect most people will be expected to work until they're much older – as everyone's living much longer.

transcript.speaker: YOUNG MAN
transcript.text: That's already happening.

transcript.speaker: YOUNG WOMAN
transcript.text: I enjoyed all that stuff on how technology has changed some jobs and how they're likely to change in the near future.

transcript.speaker: YOUNG MAN
transcript.text: Yeah, incredible. Like accountants. You might think all the technological innovations would have put them out of a job, but in fact <q id="25">there are more of them than ever. They're still really in demand and have become far more efficient.</q>

transcript.speaker: YOUNG WOMAN
transcript.text: Right. That was amazing. Twenty times more accountants in this country compared to the 19th century.

transcript.speaker: YOUNG MAN
transcript.text: I know. I'd never have thought that demand for hairdressing would have gone up so much in the last hundred years. One hairdresser for every 287 people now, compared to one for over 1,500.

transcript.speaker: YOUNG WOMAN
transcript.text: Yeah because <q id="26">people's earning power has gone up so they can afford to spend more on personal services like that.</q>

transcript.speaker: YOUNG MAN
transcript.text: But technology hasn't changed the actual job that much.

transcript.speaker: YOUNG WOMAN
transcript.text: No, they've got hairdryers, etc. but it's one job where you don't depend on a computer … The kind of work that administrative staff do has changed enormously, thanks to technology. Even 20 years ago there were secretaries doing dictation and typing.

transcript.speaker: YOUNG MAN
transcript.text: Yes. <q id="27">Really boring compared to these days, when they're given much more responsibility and higher status.</q>

transcript.speaker: YOUNG WOMAN
transcript.text: Mmm. A lot of graduates go in for this kind of work now … I'd expected there to be a much bigger change in the number of agricultural workers in the 19th century. But the 1871 census showed that roughly 25% of the population worked on the land.

transcript.speaker: YOUNG MAN
transcript.text: Yeah, <q id="28">I'd have assumed it would be more than 50%. Now it's less than 0.2%.</q>

transcript.speaker: YOUNG WOMAN
transcript.text: What about care workers?

transcript.speaker: YOUNG MAN
transcript.text: They barely existed in the 19th century as people's lifespan was so much shorter. <q id="29">But now of course this sector will see huge growth.</q>

transcript.speaker: YOUNG WOMAN
transcript.text: Yeah – and it's hard enough to meet current demand. The future looks quite bleak for bank clerks. They've been in decline since ATMs were introduced in the eighties.

transcript.speaker: YOUNG MAN
transcript.text: And <q id="30">technology will certainly make most of the jobs they do now redundant,</q> I think.

transcript.speaker: YOUNG WOMAN
transcript.text: I agree, although the situation may change. It's very hard to predict what will happen.

In today's astronomy lecture, I'm going to talk about the need for a system to manage the movement of satellites and other objects in orbit around the Earth. In other words, a Space Traffic Management system. We already have effective Air Traffic Control systems that are used internationally to ensure that planes navigate our skies safely. Well, Space Traffic Management is a similar concept, but focusing on the control of satellites.

The aim of such a system would be to prevent the danger of collisions in space between the objects in orbit around the Earth. In order to do this, <q id="31">we'd need to have a set of legal measures, and we'd also have to develop the technical systems</q> to enable us to prevent such accidents.
But unfortunately, at present we don't actually have a Space Traffic Management system that works. So why not? What are the problems in developing such a system?

Well, for one thing, <q id="32">satellites are relatively cheap these days,</q> compared with how they were in the past, meaning that more people can afford to put them into space. So there's a lot more of them out there, and people <q id="33">aren't just launching single satellites but whole constellations, consisting of thousands of them</q> designed to work together. So space is getting more crowded every day.

But in spite of this, one thing you may be surprised to learn is that you can launch a satellite into space and, once it's out there, <q id="34">it doesn't have to send back any information to Earth to allow its identification.</q> So while we have international systems for ensuring we know where the planes in our skies are, and to prevent them from colliding with one another, when it comes to the safety of satellites, <q id="35">at present we don't have anything like enough proper ways of tracking them.</q>

And it isn't just entire satellites that we need to consider. A greater threat is the huge amount of space debris in orbit around the Earth – broken bits of satellite and junk from space stations and so on. And some of these are so small that they can be very hard to identify, but they can still be very dangerous.

In addition, <q id="36">some operators may be unwilling to share information about the satellites they've launched. For example, a satellite may be designed for military purposes,</q> or it may have been launched for commercial reasons, and the operators don't want competitors to have information about it.

And even if the operators are willing to provide it, <q id="37">the information isn't easy to collect. Details are needed about the object itself, as well as about its location</q> at a particular time – and remember that a satellite isn't very big, and it's likely to be moving at thousands of kilometres an hour. We don't have any sensors that can constantly follow something moving so fast, so <q id="38">all that the scientists can do is to put forward a prediction concerning where the satellite is heading next.</q>

So those are some of the problems that we're facing. Let's consider now some of the solutions that have been suggested. One key issue is the way in which information is dealt with. We need more information, but it also needs to be accessible at a global level, so we need to establish shared standards that we can all agree on for the way in which this information is presented. We already do this in other areas of science, so although this is a challenge, it's not an impossible task. Then, as all this information's collected, it needs to be put together so it can be used, and <q id="39">that will involve creating a single database</q> on which it can be entered.

As we continue to push forward new developments, congestion of the space environment is only going to increase. To cope with this, we need to develop a system like the one I've described to coordinate the work of the numerous spacecraft operators, but <q id="40">it's also essential that this system is one that establishes trust</q> in the people that use it, both nationally and at a global level.
One interesting development …
